You're designing a part for someone to 3D print at home. They'll print it on their own printer, use only the hardware listed below, and put it together by following your manual.

## Their setup
- Printer: Bambu Lab X1C (with AMS), build volume 256 x 256 x 256 mm
- Nozzle: 0.4 mm
- Layer height: 0.2 mm
- Filament: PLA (high-speed PLA, black)
- Longest bridge seen to print cleanly on this setup: 50 mm

## Hardware they can use
Refer to an item by its catalog reference: "ISO 4762 M5x30" (socket head screw, size x length, from the lengths listed), "ISO 4032 M5" (hex nut), "ISO 10511 M5" (nylon-insert lock nut), "ISO 7089 M5" (washer), "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (1/4"-20 nut), "insert M3x4x5" (heat-set insert), "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt".

## How to work
You have these tools:
- measure(item, what): ask the person to measure one of their own things, such as their desk or their phone. They answer with what they measured, or say they can't measure it.
- submit_design(...): hand in the finished design. This ends the conversation.
- report_limitation(wanted, blocked_by, why): say you wanted to use something (a technique, a tool, a part or material, a way of handing in the design) but couldn't because of what's available here. It doesn't change anything, but it's noted.
You have at most 8 turns. Hand in a design before they run out.

## The design you hand in
submit_design's schema describes every field. The rules that matter:
- Every dimension that comes from hardware or the real world is a named param, with its source: measured (the person measured it for you), datasheet, catalog, asked (the person told you), guessed, unknown, or design (your own choice).
- Each part's `code` is Python that defines build(p) and returns a CadQuery Workplane or Shape. `cq` is already imported, and p.<name> is each param's value. Dimensions that come from hardware or the real world must come from params.
- Model each part in the orientation it's printed in, with z = 0 on the bed.
- The manual is the steps the person follows, naming the parts and hardware each step uses.

I want a hand knob for an M5 bolt, about 30 mm across, so I can tighten it without a tool. It's one printed piece. An M5 hex nut (ISO 4032) presses into the knob by hand and has to stay in when I turn the knob upside down, no glue. The nut sits fully inside the knob and can't be pushed out through the far side, and the bolt goes through the nut and out the other side.

reasoning:
I'm designing a knob with a hex nut pocket for a press-fit, working within 8 turns. The printer's tolerance will drive the fit, so a test coupon makes sense rather than measuring anything from the user. I'm sketching a knob about 30 mm across and roughly 16 mm tall, with a fluted edge for grip, and starting to lay out the hex pocket on the open bottom face.

Now I'm working out the nut pocket: an 8.0 mm across-flats hex with some press-fit clearance, about 4.7 mm deep, opened from the bottom face. The bolt hole at the top is 5.5 mm, which is smaller than the nut, so the nut can't be pushed out through it.

I'm settling how the nut stays put when the knob is flipped, since friction alone won't hold it. Printing with the open pocket facing up avoids bridging over the hex, so I'm weighing a slightly tapered mouth or a small lip near the opening to act as retention.

I'm settling on a mouth lip with a small inward step and a chamfered lead-in, so the nut can snap past it. The pocket itself will be the nut size plus a slight clearance, and I'm weighing whether hand-pressing will need more interference than that.

I'm sketching the knob's dimensions now: about 30 mm across and roughly 14 mm tall, with a 2.5 mm top ceiling. I'm also setting up a test coupon with the same pocket so the press-fit can be checked on the user's printer, and I'm noting that the hex corners are set by the circumscribed diameter, which works out to the across-flats size divided by cos 30.

I'm working through the load direction: tightening pulls the nut toward the workpiece, so the clamping force pushes the nut out through the open face against the lip rather than into the ceiling. That means the retention lip has to carry the load, not just the friction fit.

I'm reconsidering the load direction: if the open face sits on the far side from the workpiece, the nut would bear against the closed ceiling instead of the lip. The bolt would pass through the workpiece-side hole and thread into the nut above, which is the arrangement that keeps the retention lip from carrying the clamping force.

The bolt has to exit through the open top, which means the nut-depth pocket can stay open and the bolt tip just passes out of it. That removes the need for an extra bore above the nut, so the knob can be shorter, around 12 mm tall.

I'm now settling the vertical layout: the solid portion below the nut will be about 7 mm, with the nut pocket above it up to the top face. Since the printer lays the workpiece face down and the pocket opens upward, the pocket floor rests on solid material and nothing needs to bridge.

I'm checking the lip and ledge dimensions now: the hole-to-hex ledge is about 1.25 mm wide, which is enough for the nut flat to sit on. The bottom edge will get a small chamfer to handle elephant foot, and the pocket depth comes out to roughly the nut height plus slack, with the retention lip sitting just above the nut top.

I'm settling the pocket sizing now: a main pocket about 8.2 mm across flats for the 8.0 mm nut, with a little clearance, and a tighter lip to hold it. I'm weighing whether the hex needs to be snug enough to resist the nut turning, since the clamping torque is shared across the flats.

I'm checking whether the lip can flex enough for a hand press: the nut's corners would interfere with a lip sized to 7.7 mm across flats, and a thin 0.8 mm PLA ring won't give much, so the push-in force could be substantial.

I'm turning the lip into three small ribs on alternating flats instead of a continuous ring, since a full ring is too stiff to flex for a hand press. The ribs would protrude about 0.25 mm inward and have a lead-in chamfer, and I'm working out where each flat's midpoint sits so I can place them.

Now I'm writing the rib geometry as an extruded trapezoid profile in the radial-z plane, with a lead-in chamfer at the top.

Still writing the rib profile...

Now I'm settling the rib details: a protrusion of about 0.25 mm, a 2.5 mm width, and a lead-in slope at the top, with the bolt clearance hole kept as a parameter at 5.5 mm and the knob's outer diameter set to 30 mm.

Still working out the scalloped grip: ten cutouts on the 30 mm outer edge, and I'm checking the wall stays thick enough around the hex corners. Next I'm noting the catalog M5 nut and bolt values I'm building from, then sizing a test coupon with a shorter cylinder carrying the same pocket.

I'm weighing whether to include a bolt in the hardware list, since the user only mentioned having an M5 bolt without a length. I'm leaning toward listing a fastener with an assumed length and noting it, rather than leaving the joint without an identifier.

I'm settling the joint definitions now: the knob gets a bolt-hole clearance feature and a nut pocket feature, with the axis running along z from the origin. The bolt head sits on the far side of the workpiece, so the head isn't seated in the knob and I don't need a separate head-seat role. I'm also starting on the criteria, checking that the nut pocket contains the nut and that the bolt hole clears the bolt.

I'm now defining the parameters: a nut across flats of 8.0 mm, a bolt diameter of 5 mm, a 30 mm knob with a 12 mm height, and a pocket depth that comes to the nut height plus the rib gap and rib height.

Still writing the knob code...

Still writing the knob code...

Still writing the rib code...

Still writing the pocket and coupon code...

I'm settling the print orientation: the workpiece face goes on the bed with the pocket opening upward. I'll submit now, leave the questions field optional, and skip the measurement step. I'll also add a note recommending PLA and four to five walls.
